own_comprehension.problem: Recognizing each character does not guarantee a correct full-page transcription. A full transcription must also keep the reading order and row boundaries required by the task.
own_comprehension.example: The reference shopping list is milk on the first row and bread on the second. Reversing the rows keeps the four Chinese characters and the one newline, but changes the answer order.
own_comprehension.code: Counter converts each string into counts per character and ignores positions. Comparing the two Counters with == returns True for the row-swap input. Comparing the raw strings with == returns False because their positions differ. The literal \n is a newline; splitlines() returns rows in the order already present in the string, making the swap visible.
own_comprehension.numbers_and_symbols: There are four Chinese characters and one newline in each original string, and two rows in each splitlines result. == is equality comparison, not a rule that repairs order. The assigned section contains no mathematical formula. The linked prerequisite's five-character example has one different character, producing 1/5 = 0.2; that code was read but not run for this assignment.
own_comprehension.exercise: With predicted = 牛奶麵包, all four Chinese characters and their within-string sequence are correct, but the row boundary is gone. Counter now also detects the missing newline. Ignoring all whitespace makes the flattened strings equal, so that equality cannot prove preservation of the original page structure. A two-column receipt needs a predeclared reading convention to decide whether to follow each column or cross the page row by row.
own_comprehension.cropping: A crop can make small characters easier to see but removes the location that tells us where they belong on the page. Recognizing text regions and organizing a whole page are distinct tasks, so a recognition score alone is insufficient evidence of a general layout capability.
